lines.trans: Hey there, excuse me, my friend. Would you help me real quick?
I cannot, I do not have spare change, pal.
It is not money, no. It is just a real favor.
I promise not to take up your time.
Okay, go ahead.
I would like to know if you can be my guarantor, sir.
Be a guarantor?
I rented a great apartment just now, recently.
If those people over there find out, they will grab it ahead of me.
Which people? The people living on the street?
We do not like to be called that.

words.gram: feminine singular article in a gente

lines.trans: See you soon!

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Support needed from a coworker, often in precisar da ajuda de alguém.

examples.text: Ela precisa da ajuda do colega.
examples.trans: She needs her colleague's help.
Thanks for the help!

meanings.note: Common everyday verb for offering or asking for assistance.

examples.trans: I am going to help you.
Can you help me?

meanings.note: Used both for renting from a landlord and renting out.

examples.trans: I rented a great apartment.
They want to rent a house.

meanings.note: Standard Brazilian word for an apartment unit.

examples.trans: I rented a great apartment.
The landlord sold the apartment.

meanings.note: Points to manner or way.

examples.text: A gente não gosta de ser chamada assim.
examples.trans: We do not like to be called that.
No, leave it like that.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.

examples.trans: See you later!
See you later. Thanks!

meanings.note: Adds immediacy after imperatives like calma aí, or means there near you.

examples.trans: Hang on!
Who is there?

meanings.note: In the passive ser chamado, means to be called by a label.

examples.text: A gente não gosta de ser chamada assim.
examples.trans: We do not like to be called that.
What is your name?

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.trans: I want coffee with sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.
examples.trans: She is with our team.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.

examples.trans: It’s a marketing meeting.
I’m in finance.

meanings.note: General term for money.

examples.trans: It is not money, no.
I have no money right now.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.

examples.trans: He is in the meeting.
She stays on her phone.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
I’m not going.

meanings.note: Covers speaking, talking, and telling in everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.
examples.trans: Let me tell you something.
They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: A lease guarantor who co-signs a Brazilian rental contract.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?
Everyone is looking for a guarantor.

meanings.note: Used in na frente de (in front of someone).

examples.text: Não grita na frente dos outros!
examples.trans: Don't shout in front of everyone else!

examples.text: Te espero na frente da sala.
examples.trans: I'll wait for you in front of the room.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Conditional eu gostaria softens a refusal (I would like to, but...).

examples.trans: I would like to, but I have work.
I really like this team.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: In com licença, the polite phrase for asking to pass or interrupt.

examples.trans: Hey there, excuse me, my friend.
Excuse me, may I come in?

meanings.note: In the farewell até logo it anticipates meeting again. This is the time adverb, not a short form for a company logo.

examples.trans: See you later!
I’ll go to the meeting soon.

meanings.note: First-person singular object clitic.

examples.trans: Would you help me real quick?

examples.text: Por favor, me deixa morar aqui!
examples.trans: Please let me live here!

meanings.note: Between article and noun (a mesma coisa) it means the same.

examples.trans: It's the same thing.
We work on the same team.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
That is my job.

meanings.note: In morador de rua, a person living on the street.

examples.trans: The homeless residents?
The building's residents complained.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.

examples.trans: No, I’m not going.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: What is your job title?
Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Friendly, upbeat Brazilian greeting or attention-getter.

examples.trans: Hey there, excuse me, my friend.
Hey there, it is me again.

meanings.note: Used for taking transport, grabbing items, or taking an apartment first.

examples.trans: They will grab it ahead of me.
I do not need to take the subway.

poder.gloss: can; may; to be able to

meanings.en: can; may; to be able to
meanings.note: Core modal verb followed by an infinitive.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?
I cannot right now.

meanings.note: In colloquial Brazilian speech, esse povo means 'these people / that crowd'.

examples.text: Se esse povo aí souber, vai pegar.
examples.trans: If those people over there find out, they will take it.
Which people?

meanings.note: Followed directly by an infinitive or que.

examples.text: Prometo não tomar o seu tempo.
examples.trans: I promise not to take up your time.
He promised to help.

meanings.note: Interrogative pronoun for people.

examples.trans: Which people, who?
Who said that?

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Is that what you want?

meanings.note: Warm Brazilian vocative used even with strangers.

examples.trans: Excuse me, my friend.
I do not have change, pal.

meanings.note: Diminutive of rápido used adverbially in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Would you help me real quick?
I will sort this out real quick.

meanings.note: Formed from recente + -mente.

examples.trans: I rented an apartment just now, recently.
We moved here recently.

meanings.note: Public street.

examples.text: Meu amigo na rua finge que não me vê.
examples.trans: My friend on the street pretends not to see me.
The street is quiet today.

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Do you know the answer?

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Polite title; saying sim, senhor to an equal coworker adds mock military obedience.

examples.trans: Yes, sir.
Are you going in now, sir?

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
It’s a marketing meeting.

meanings.note: Possessive determiner agreeing with the possessed noun; in Brazil it most often means your (with você).

examples.trans: What is your job title?

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

meanings.note: Limits a statement (eu só quero) or forms só que (except that / the catch is).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

examples.text: Só que agora ela precisa de ajuda.
examples.trans: Except now she needs help.

meanings.note: Refers to someone's time or duration (esse tempo inteiro).

examples.text: Seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
I stayed there that whole time.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Standard verb for having coffee, tea, water, or soup.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
I have coffee in the morning.

meanings.note: Coins or small bills.

examples.trans: I do not have spare change, pal.
Do you have small change for the bus?

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Superlative-strength everyday word for 'great'.

examples.trans: Look, it went great!
I rented a great apartment.
